author: Kelly Milan
title: Tennessee Secretary of State spurs book checks across Middle Tennessee; raising new questions over state oversight - NewsBreak
text:
By Kelly Milan ,
42 minutes ago
SUMNER COUNTY, Tenn. (WKRN) — What began as a series of sudden “emergency closures” at Rutherford County libraries is now emerging as part of a broader directive from Tennessee’s Secretary of State, which reached into Sumner County and may soon extend to other library systems across Middle Tennessee.
Sumner County officials confirmed this week that they received a letter from Secretary of State Tre Hargett instructing libraries to launch an “immediate age-appropriateness review” of all juvenile materials. The directive, according to the letter, is aimed at ensuring compliance with federal law, Tennessee’s new age-appropriateness statute and a Trump-era executive order concerning “gender ideology.”
RELATED | Rutherford County libraries close amid book reviews The order gives library systems 60 days to review every book in their children’s and juvenile sections, defined as material for readers 12 and under. A full report must be submitted to the Tennessee State Librarian and Archivist by Jan. 19, 2026, summarizing any titles deemed inappropriate and detailing what action was taken.
In the letter, Hargett writes that he is “keenly aware” of the need to ensure federal and state funding is not jeopardized “due to potential misuse by an individual library or librarian,” adding that he “cannot allow the actions of one library to impact over 200 libraries in the state.”
The directive drew a packed audience at the Sumner County Library Board’s meeting Wednesday night, where residents lined up to offer sharply divided views.
One parent raised concerns about a young adult novel depicting a transgender teenager, saying, “It’s a book about a girl changing gender to be a male so she can swim. The drawing in the front shows two scars, deep, long scars for a mastectomy and another scar for a hysterectomy, so we are talking about some serious stuff in here. I am not saying it is graphic or pornographic in here. I am saying this person is cutting off healthy body parts to become something he is not born into.”
Board members themselves acknowledged the ambiguity in the state’s terminology.
“What I’m seeing looks like a general age-appropriateness review,” one member said. “That could mean one book comes out of a section or 20. We need more direction from the state librarian.”
The review requirements follow a similar closure and inventory sweep in Rutherford County, where multiple branches temporarily shut their doors last week. Those closures were attributed to “state reporting requirements” connected to Hargett’s office.
⏩ Read today’s top stories on wkrn.com
As more library systems acknowledge receiving the directive or await clarification, the central question remains: Is this a statewide routine audit, or the beginning of a new political battle over which books Tennessee’s youngest readers can access?
The Sumner County Library Board is scheduled to meet again on Jan. 14, 2026, unless a special session is called before then.
